title: The Polymath Who Invented Inoculation
event_summary: In 1721, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of the British ambassador to Constantinople, championed the Ottoman practice of variolation—deliberately infecting patients with material from mild smallpox cases to build immunity—which she had witnessed being performed by elderly women in Istanbul's markets as early as 1717. She had her own children inoculated by embassy surgeon Charles Maitland and upon returning to London publicly campaigned for its adoption, facing fierce resistance from the medical establishment and the Church. Simultaneously, an enslaved West African man named Onesimus told Cotton Mather in Boston that he had been inoculated in Africa as a child using the same technique, prompting Mather and Dr. Zabdiel Boylston to inoculate 242 Bostonians during a deadly epidemic—proving statistically for the first time that inoculation dramatically reduced mortality.
why_forgotten: Western medical history overwhelmingly credits Edward Jenner's later cowpox vaccine of 1796, eclipsing the Ottoman and African origins of the entire concept. The idea that enslaved Africans and Ottoman women possessed superior medical knowledge was deeply uncomfortable for Enlightenment-era Europeans invested in narratives of Western scientific supremacy. Onesimus's contribution in particular was systematically minimized because crediting an enslaved person with saving a colonial city undermined the ideological foundations of slavery itself.
why_it_matters: The 1721 Boston inoculation campaign was history's first controlled public health experiment using statistical evidence, establishing the methodology that underpins all modern clinical trials. Without the cross-cultural transmission of African and Ottoman folk immunology to Europe, the entire trajectory of vaccination—from Jenner to Pasteur to modern mRNA vaccines—might have been delayed by generations. It remains one of the most powerful examples of non-Western medical knowledge reshaping global science.
